candidates.title: Empirical evaluation of generate→verify→repair loops with deterministic network validators
candidates.research_question: How much does integrating a deterministic network validator into an LLM-driven generate→verify→repair pipeline reduce actionable misconfiguration rates across diverse synthetic vendor/topology tasks compared to LLM-only outputs?
hypotheses: Integrating a deterministic validator into the LLM generate→verify→repair loop reduces final actionable misconfiguration rate by at least 50% relative to unchecked LLM outputs on the same task set.
Residual errors after automated repair will be disproportionately policy- or intent-mismatch errors (semantic) rather than syntactic/parse errors.
candidates.proposed_design: Preregistered paired experiment using a fixed task bank of 200 NetOps intent-to-configuration tasks across three vendor families (Cisco-like, Juniper-like, neutral RFC-style). For each task: (1) call an LLM prompt to produce a configuration change; (2) run validator (Batfish-style deterministic checks) to report failures; (3) allow the LLM a single automated repair attempt using validator feedback; (4) record syntactic/semantic error labels. Compare LLM-only (no validator/repair) vs LLM+validator+repair on same seed tasks. Use public synthetic topologies and configuration templates; run all calls via hosted-model API with fixed seeds and store full logs. Stopping rules and retry policy frozen in preregistration.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task records: raw LLM config, validator failure messages, repaired config, binary final-actionable-error label, error-type taxonomy (syntax/semantic/policy), repair success flag, timestamps, model-call counts. Aggregated counts: initial error rate, post-repair error rate, repair-success rate, distribution of error types, per-vendor breakdown.
candidates.primary_outcome: Absolute and relative reduction in actionable misconfiguration rate (proportion) after one validator-guided repair attempt (paired comparison).
candidates.analysis_outline: Primary analysis: paired proportion test (McNemar or paired bootstrap) comparing initial vs post-repair actionable-error proportions; report absolute reduction, 95% CI, and p-value. Secondary: per-vendor stratified comparisons, error-type contingency tables (Chi-square), repair-success predictors via logistic regression (features: task complexity, vendor, initial error type). Report effect sizes, sample-size power calculation, and failure-mode qualitative synthesis with example cases.
risks: Validator coverage gaps leading to false negatives (undetected unsafe configs)
LLM repair may overfit to validator messages producing superficially valid but semantically incorrect configs
Synthetic vendor models may not fully capture production vendor idiosyncrasies
Possible API rate or cost limits requiring truncation of planned sample

candidates.title: Vulnerability of NetOps RAG pipelines to adversarially poisoned retrieval contexts
candidates.research_question: To what extent can adversarially poisoned documents added to a NetOps retrieval corpus induce LLM-generated actionable misconfigurations in an otherwise benign RAG pipeline?
hypotheses: Injecting a single high-impact adversarial document into a RAG index will significantly increase the rate of actionable misconfigurations produced by the LLM vs an unpoisoned index.
The induced misconfigurations will correlate with the similarity between task intent and poisoned-document surface cues (higher similarity → higher attack success).
candidates.proposed_design: Controlled adversarial experiment using a frozen RAG pipeline: build a retrieval index from public NetOps docs (vendor guides, runbooks). Define 100 intent tasks. For each task run three conditions (paired within-task): (A) clean index; (B) index with a benign distractor doc; (C) index with a crafted poisoned doc that contains subtle malicious instructions contradicting best-practice (but syntactically plausible). For each retrieval context, run identical LLM prompt template; evaluate produced configs using deterministic validator and semantic checks in simulator (no real devices). Measure actionable-misconfig proportion per condition. Vary poison strength and insertion rank in additional ablations. Ethical safeguards: all execution in isolated simulator and synthetic topologies; poison content non-deployable to real networks.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task/control condition: retrieval hits, poisoned-doc presence/rank, LLM output, validator failure flags, semantic-safety flag, attack-success binary. Aggregates: misconfig rates per condition, attack-success vs poison-rank curve, similarity correlation metrics.
candidates.primary_outcome: Increase in actionable-misconfiguration proportion in poisoned vs clean retrieval conditions (difference in proportions with 95% CI).
candidates.analysis_outline: Primary: paired proportion tests across conditions (McNemar or paired bootstrap). Dose-response analysis: logistic regression of attack success vs poisoned-doc rank/similarity. Sensitivity analysis across poison templates and retrieval settings. Report false-positive/false-negative validator rates under poisoning. Include adversarial-case qualitative examples.
risks: Ethical risk of producing deployable malicious payloads (mitigated by simulator-only execution and non-deployable poison phrasing)
Indexer/retrieval artifacts may not reflect enterprise document heterogeneity
Attack strength dependent on chosen poison templates; may under- or over-estimate real-world vulnerability

candidates.title: Evaluating confidence-calibration methods as automated gates for NetOps action approval
candidates.research_question: Can post-hoc calibration methods applied to LLM outputs produce reliable gating thresholds (approve/reject) for automatic NetOps actions while maintaining acceptable coverage and low false-accept rates?
hypotheses: A calibrated confidence estimator (temperature scaling or ensemble Brier reduction) achieves a usable operating point where false-accept rate ≤5% while retaining ≥40% automated-apply coverage on the task bank.

Different calibration methods will produce statistically different trade-offs between coverage and false-accept rate, with ensembles outperforming single-model temperature scaling on calibration metrics (ECE, Brier).
candidates.proposed_design: Generate a 300-task NetOps intent bank. For each task, obtain LLM config and an intrinsic model-provided logit/confidence signal where available; if unavailable, compute proxy scores (model log-probability of generated token sequence). Split dataset into calibration (60%) and evaluation (40%). Fit calibration methods on calibration set: temperature scaling, isotonic regression, Platt, ensemble averaging (if multiple model variants available). Define gating thresholds (range) and evaluate on held-out tasks: measure coverage (proportion of tasks above threshold) and false-accept rate (validator-flagged actionable errors among approved items). Produce ROC-style and decision-curve plots and compute ECE/Brier.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task: raw model-score, calibrated probability, validator correctness, approval decision at multiple thresholds. Aggregates: coverage vs false-accept tradeoff curves, calibration metrics (ECE, Brier), threshold operating points achieving policy targets.
candidates.primary_outcome: Calibration method and threshold achieving false-accept rate ≤5% with maximal coverage; report coverage and uncertainty (95% CI).
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute calibration metrics (ECE, Brier) per method; compute decision operating points and compare coverage using bootstrapped CIs. Use paired comparisons across methods (Wilcoxon or paired t on coverage at fixed FPR). Produce calibration plots and decision-curve analysis. Report sample-size-driven uncertainty and robustness to task subgroups.
risks: Model score proxies may poorly reflect true uncertainty leading to optimistic calibration
Calibration may not generalize across vendors or task types (distribution shift)
Coverage targets might be unattainable without unacceptably high false-accept rates

candidates.title: Design and evaluation of a reproducible multi-vendor NetOps benchmark and evaluation pipeline
candidates.research_question: Does a curated, publicly reproducible benchmark corpus with end-to-end execution and deterministic verification reveal operational LLM failure modes that are not captured by prior knowledge-style evaluations?
hypotheses: A multi-vendor, end-to-end benchmark with deterministic verification will show a substantially different failure-mode distribution (higher semantic/policy error share) than knowledge-only question benchmarks.

Publishing a standardized benchmark and evaluation pipeline will produce reproducible per-task failure logs that enable consistent comparison across models and prompt variants and will facilitate discovery of previously underreported failure modes (e.g., rollback omission).
candidates.proposed_design: Assemble a benchmark of 250 intent-to-configuration tasks covering multiple vendor families and operational scenarios (routing changes, ACLs, NAT, BGP policies). Provide synthetic topology files, configuration templates, and deterministic validators/simulators. Define standard prompts, scoring rules (syntax, pass/fail validator, semantic policy match), and data formats. Run an initial baseline evaluation using two LLM prompting strategies and report per-task metrics and failure taxonomy. Publish corpus and evaluation code under permissive license. Use only public data sources and synthetic artifacts.
candidates.expected_data: Benchmark artifacts (topologies, intents), per-task model outputs, validator results, error taxonomy counts, per-model aggregated metrics, reproducible logs and hashes. Comparison between benchmark-derived failure distribution and that from a knowledge-style benchmark (e.g., existing NetOps QA dataset) on overlapping tasks.
candidates.primary_outcome: Demonstration that the benchmark reveals a distinct, reproducible distribution of operational failure modes (quantified difference in semantic/policy error proportion with 95% CI) and a working open evaluation pipeline.
candidates.analysis_outline: Descriptive statistics of per-task pass/fail rates, error-type proportions; cluster analysis of failure modes; paired comparison where tasks overlap with knowledge benchmarks (difference in semantic-error proportions with bootstrapped CI). Provide reproducibility checklist and exemplar reproducibility hashes for artifacts.
risks: Licensing and provenance concerns for included public artifacts
Synthetic benchmark may still miss production idiosyncrasies limiting external validity
Resource cost to evaluate many models/prompts may exceed modest budgets
